speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY MESSAGE OF PRESIDENT ROOSEVELT TO SEAWAY AND POWER CONFERENCE-ENGINEERING PROBLEMS IN INTERNATIONAL SECTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are called I should like to ask a question of the Prime Minister	(Mr. Mackenzie King). In view of President Roosevelt's message to the Great Lakes seaway and power conference yesterday, in which he is reported to have emphasized, among other things, " that the St. Lawrence project would provide millions in new horsepower urgently needed to speed up defence production," will the Prime Minister make a statement outlining in general terms the progress that has been made from the Canadian standpoint with respect to the scheme advocated by the Canadian representatives on the joint board as between (a) a singlestage development, (b) a double-stage development, (c) a controlled single-stage, or other scheme?
Will the Prime Minister also state what is the attitude of the government with respect to the seaway proposal, and whether opportunity will be given to those whose property will be adversely affected by the choice of scheme to present their views?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY MESSAGE OF PRESIDENT ROOSEVELT TO SEAWAY AND POWER CONFERENCE-ENGINEERING PROBLEMS IN INTERNATIONAL SECTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend advised me of his intention to ask the question he has. I had anticipated that some question would be asked with respect to the important message which the President of the United States issued yesterday through Mr. Berle in connection with a great lakes seaway and power conference which is being held in Detroit. I have therefore come prepared to make a brief reply to my hon. friend.
The house has already been advised through the correspondence tabled on November 12 of the agreement reached between the government of Canada and the government of the United States, regarding additional diversion of water for power purposes at Niagara and the appointment of committees to carry on the necessary additional engineering investigations in the international rapids section of the St.

St. Lawrence Waterway
Lawrence. The diversion has been made at Niagara and the power development is being utilized for Canadian industry. The committees appointed by the two governments have been actively at work in the study and analysis of the engineering problems in the international section.
As regards the wider questions involved in the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence development, it will be recalled that the Niagara convention of 1929 and the St. Lawrence treaty of 1932 failed to obtain the approval of the United States senate, and the negotiations were later resumed with a view to the possibility of combining the projects in a revised single agreement. Delegations of officials appointed by the two governments met in Ottawa and in Washington last January and the problems involved have continued to receive consideration by both governments. Those negotiations will be continued. Any agreement resulting from the negotiations will, of course, be submitted to this house for approval in due course. I have earlier indicated that any such agreement on this subject would not be brought before the Canadian parliament until it had received the approval of the appropriate United States authorities.
As I have already indicated, the committees appointed by the two governments are continuing their study of the engineering problems in the international section. They have not yet completed or reported upon their work, and no final decision has therefore been taken as to the details of the development in this section. The project under consideration, as I stated a few days ago, is a controlled single-stage development, which differs from either the single-stage development or the double-stage development that was under consideration some .ten years ago. On January 25 last the following statement as to the character of the project under discussion was issued after the conference of officials of the two governments:
The engineering advisers of the two governments have reached substantial agreement on the feasibility and desirability of a project in the international rapids section of the St. Lawrence river which would involve a main dam in the vicinity of Barnhart island, with a power house in each country, and a control dam upstream. This project is based upon a plan which was discussed in some detail in the 1926 report of the joint board of engineers. The engineers of the two countries are in agreement that such a project is sound from an engineering standpoint, cheaper in cost than the project on which the 1932 treaty was based, and affords full protection for all the interests in the various sections of the St. Lawrence river.
My hon. friend the member for Grenville-Dundas has inquired whether opportunity will be given to those whose property will be adversely affected by the choice of scheme, to present their views. Any scheme for development naturally affects some adjoining property. This was of course true of the project embodied in the treaty which was negotiated by the government of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett in 1932. At the appropriate time the present government will be quite prepared to receive representations from those whose property will be adversely or, for that matter, beneficially affected.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was good enough to read to the house a copy of a telegram that he had sent to Doctor Robert McClure. The press reports that Doctor McClure has replied to the Prime Minister, and I wonder whether

Nickel and Scrap Iron
the Prime Minister would care to place that reply on the record and give the assurance requested?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: EXPLANATION OF DOCTOR ROBERT MCCLURE OF REPORTED STATEMENT AS TO SHIPMENTS TO JAPAN
speechtext:
I may say to my hon. friend that I am more than pleased to meet his request; for I certainly had in mind placing the telegram of Doctor McClure on Hansard to-day. It deserves something in the way of attention.
The house is already aware of the statement which was made by Doctor McClure at Toronto with respect to the export of nickel and of the fact that the Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs sent a telegram to Doctor McClure asking for an explanation of his statement and requesting particularly information as to the source from which he got his information. The following is the reply which the Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs has received:
Toronto, Ont., December 5, 1940. Dr. O. D. Skelton,
Under-Secretary of State for
External Affairs,
Ottawa.
In view of the disturbing reports I have been given from what I consider an authority, and in view* also of persistent rumours which have been given credence by less informed persons, I believe it would be in the best interest of Canada and the empire if you would unequivocally state that in addition to no permits being granted for the direct export from Canada to J apan of nickel, every precaution has been taken to ensure that no Canadian nickel, in any form whatsoever, is finding its way, even circuitously, to Japan or to any country dominated by or friendly to Japan from which transshipment might be made. I think your statement also should apply to Canadian copper in all forms and to zinc and lead. I do know from the disquiet in certain circles in China, Canada and United States that such a comprehensive, unequivocal statement would allay many fears. The information which I consider authoritative and on which I based my statement was not to the effect that shipments of Canadian nickel were being made directly from Canada to Japan but that they were reaching Japan after having been shipped from Canada to some other nations, such as United States or to some Pacific nations dominated by Japan. If the facts permit you to state that such transshipments do not occur, I will be most happy to apologize fully for having added to your cares at this time. Arriving Ottawa Friday evening.
McClure.
I might say to Doctor McClure that his apology is owing rather to the British government and to the other governments of the British commonwealth of nations for adding to the very difficult situation which at the present time exists between the governments of the different parts of the empire and other governments in the orient. These are days in which language cannot be too greatly
restrained, and the language used by Doctor McClure in his statement which I quoted yesterday was of a character to raise very considerable difficulties between the governments of the British commonwealth of nations and certain countries in the orient.
The communication I have read to-day, while it does not answer the one sent yesterday, is very different in its statement from the one which was made originally. It is now not direct shipments to Japan, but it is said that nickel may have been sent from Canada to some other country and have found its way from that other country around to Japan. The statement originally made by Doctor McClure was that he himself had been digging scrap iron which had come from Canada out of the bodies of Chinese and that he expected others would be digging nickel which came from Canada out of the bodies of British soldiers. That is a very different indictment from that which appears in his telegram that I have just read.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: EXPLANATION OF DOCTOR ROBERT MCCLURE OF REPORTED STATEMENT AS TO SHIPMENTS TO JAPAN
speechtext: He did not say they were direct shipments; I think I should say that in justice to Doctor McClure. I do not know him at all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: EXPLANATION OF DOCTOR ROBERT MCCLURE OF REPORTED STATEMENT AS TO SHIPMENTS TO JAPAN
speechtext: No, he did not. He did not say they were not direct shipments.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: EXPLANATION OF DOCTOR ROBERT MCCLURE OF REPORTED STATEMENT AS TO SHIPMENTS TO JAPAN
speechtext:

inference was clear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: EXPLANATION OF DOCTOR ROBERT MCCLURE OF REPORTED STATEMENT AS TO SHIPMENTS TO JAPAN
speechtext:
Now, instead of Doctor McClure having information of his own knowledge, he states that his remarks were based on a statement which was made by some unnamed Canadian official and on information from some United States committee. Doctor McClure is to be in Ottawa, I understand, either this afternoon or to-morrow, and I have asked the Undersecretary of State to ascertain from him the name of the Canadian official who he says gave him this information, and also to enlighten us a little as to the United States committee that gave the information on which he based the extraordinary statement which he made.
I have already given the house information as to the export of nickel from Canada. Its export has been under extremely close control since the beginning of the war. Permits are required for its shipment from this country in any form to any destination, and permits have not been granted when there was any reason to believe that the nickel might directly or indirectly reach a hostile destination.
We have not only made certain that no nickel was exported direct from Canada to any dangerous or possibly dangerous destina-

Nickel and Scrap Iron

tion, but we have taken far-reaching precautions to see that nickel exported from Canada to another country is not re-exported in primary or fabricated form to any destination for which we would not grant an export permit for nickel in the first place. Our policy, as I have already stated, is to see that nickel is kept to meet the war needs of Britain, direct, and in articles being manufactured for Britain and ourselves in the United States. It is obvious that the secondary control cannot be as completely watertight as is our direct control over the shipment of nickel in its primary forms. Nevertheless, I have reason to believe that it is operating satisfactorily except with regard to nickel scrap. Here there is undoubtedly a small reexport trade from other countries to which the Canadian system of export control and guarantees cannot be extended.
I might add that I am prepared to arrange to have any member of the house furnished with full confidential information as to the control procedure in force in Canada, but it would not be advisable to make that particular aspect of the question public.

speechtext:
I wish to say a word on a matter which I do not think can be called one of parliamentary privilege, and certainly it is not a matter of personal privilege, but it might be as well to clear it up.

I notice that the Montreal Gazette of to-day contains an editorial in which it finds difficulty in seeing why it should be necessary for this government to confer with the British government before deciding whether or not we should resume our sittings on the 17th of February. The language used in my motion respecting adjournment, on which the editorial is based, was that you, Mr. Speaker, in conference with his majesty's government, would decide whether or not it was necessary to have parliament reassemble earlier than February 17. The Gazette seems still to belong to an age which regards his majesty's government as the government existing in Great Britain. I might say that over thirty years ago Sir Wilfrid Laurier made clear to all parts of the empire that the governments of the different dominions were all his majesty's governments. Certainly for many years past, in official communications which have passed between the governments of Great Britain and Canada, the one is referred to as "His Majesty's Government in the United Kingdom," and the other as "His Majesty's Government in Canada." That is the present practice. When I speak of "his majesty's government," if I not specify, I have reference to His Majesty's Government in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am quite content, Mr. Chairman, to have the resolution carry, but an hon. member asked that I make a statement with regard to it before it was considered by the house. In the speech which I made at the time these proposals were introduced I emphasized the extent to which the government is in a positive way attempting to increase our supplies of foreign exchange. We are not confining ourselves merely to negative, restrictive measures. The present provision as to encouragement of exports is in the nature of an enabling measure. It gives power to the governor in council to enter into agreements. It is anticipated that under such agreements the government would offer certain concessions in exchange for an undertaking on the part of a company or individual to provide additional exchange of some amount. The benefits would be conditional upon a certain undertaking having been fulfilled by the exporter to the government's advantage.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is, to increase their exports?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. While this method of proceeding may be regarded as unusual, I think it is fully justified by the unusual circumstances we have to face. The variety of situations with which we may have to deal makes it next to impossible to formulate legislation which will be sufficiently elastic. I should like to give the house an example of what I mean by this.

War Exchange Conservation Act
A company may be able, through certain additional capital expenditure, say to double its exports of pulp. If it did this it would probably find that 79-5 per cent of its profits on this business would be taken away in corporation income tax and excess profits tax. In British Columbia, for example,- a further ten per cent of profits would be taken by the provincial government if the profits exceeded a certain amount. In these circumstances the company would have only 10 * 5 per cent of its profits left. This margin of profits might not be sufficient to justify the capital expenditure for what might later have proved to be only a temporary market. In such a case a greater allowance for depreciation than is ordinarily allowed might be sufficient to induce the company to go ahead and take the risks involved. Another company might be able to expand somewhat its exports with little or no additional capital expenditure. Additional depreciation might not be of great assistance here. Different circumstances in this case might call for another type of incentive.
It is just possible after we have explored the possibilities further we may be able to generalize on some incentive provisions for certain industries. And here I might again emphasize that this is enabling legislation that we are concerned with. I would interject at this point that it was at first contemplated that we would ask the house for power to finance, to assist industries by loan or guarantee, if they would undertake to provide a certain amount of foreign exchange.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: We really do not need that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I thought it was too dangerous a power for the government to take and that the two classes of assistance authorized by this bill were sufficient, at least to start with. There are two classes, one being increased depreciation or depletion allowance, and the other tax credits, which would be proportioned to the exchange produced.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister has abandoned that idea?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Of financing?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
If you
allow these companies to make a little money they will do their own financing. It should not in any degree become a burden on the country's credit.
[MY. Ilsley.]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I argued that the companies should be allowed to make a little money this last year, and my hon. friend was in favour of a 100 per cent excess profits tax.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Based on the English practice. Do away with the corporation tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They would not have had any incentive then. In other industries, it may not be possible even subsequently to lay down any general rules. For example, certain gold mines may be facing a situation where the margin of profit is so low-for instances, 50 cents a ton-that it is not in the interests of the company to attempt to continue operations. I think anyone who is familiar with the gold mining industry will realize that some mines can continue to look forward to a profitable future even with a very low rate of profit per ton, while in other cases a much higher rate of profit per ton may not be sufficient to justify continuing operations. In circumstances such as these, the house will realize that it would be uneconomical to offer concessions to all mines whose profit per ton is less than a certain amount. An arrangement of this sort would almost necessarily mean that many would be getting benefits which they do not need, while others which needed it were obtaining no relief whatever. It is in the face of situations such as these that it seemed necessary to take power to deal with individuals by means of contract or agreement rather than attempt the more wasteful and uneconomical method of providing benefits through general legislation.
It is the intention of the government to have such agreements as are entered into tabled in the house and available to members. Full details with regard to the administration of this provision have not yet been worked out. However, these details will be developed later as seems best.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Would
they be made available in the interim if parliament were not in session? They will be stale by the time we get back. As regards the question of depreciation and depletion, to which the minister has alluded, has he come to any conclusion with respect to the extra quantum of depreciation and depletion which may be allowed? Both are important. I am not opposing the suggestion at the moment, but I should like to have it elucidated.
I would point out, on the subject of depreciation, that consideration ought to be given the question whether the raw material is cut off a company's licensed lands, that is to say, lands held under licence from a provincial government, or whether the raw material is cut off

War Exchange Conservation Act
freehold lands owned by the company. May I tell the minister my own experience? Not so very long ago, in settling a tax claim against a taxpayer, I discovered that in the income tax department no discrimination was made, on the item of depletion, between pulp-wood cut on licensed land held under a licence from the crown in the right of one of the provinces and raw material cut on the company's privately-owned lands held in fee simple. The situations are entirely different. This was some time ago, and apparently the department had not before had the matter drawn to their attention. They adopted an arbitrary figure, say a dollar a cord

I cannot remember the exact figures-and applied it in both cases, whereas in the case of privately-owned land double depletion at least should be allowed on raw material cut on fee simple land owned by the company. The land can be cropped only once in so many years. There is not the capital invested in a timber licence that there is in privately-owned land, and if they are to be on the same basis it will work an injustice. Much greater depletion should be allowed for pulpwood cut on fee simple land than on licensed land. I am sure I convinced the commissioner that this was the proper thing to do and I hope he has been following out that practice. I wish to take time by the forelock to suggest that it be carried out.
Since we were here last evening there has appeared in the morning papers-I have before me a clipping from the Ottawa Journal of this date-an item which I suppose was supplied by the Canadian Press. The heading is:
Gov't to Aid Newsprint Industry
May give tax relief under special war measure.
The text reads:
The government is expected to take action, probably under a provision in the special war finance measures now before parliament, to give taxation relief to the newsprint industry.
This industry to-day ranks next to gold in commodity export to the United States and thus in the provision of the urgently needed United States dollars.
It goes on to tell a story and to give figures of exports, and it refers to the minister's speech on Monday in which he spoke of a "special allowance for depreciation or depletion of capital assets" being made to companies for the purpose of export trade. It adds:
That is a provision which may be worked out under the Excess Profits Tax Act.
May I ask the -minister if it is intended to do that through that legislation or by enabling legislation such as he has now referred to in connection with the matter at present under consideration?
I should like to make this statement with respect to the excess profits tax. Perhaps it is too late to start off on a new basis in connection with that tax; we have had for years the corporation tax. This is the thought I should like to convey to the minister: that these companies should not be taxed to death at the present time; they must be sound and able to withstand the depression that may come to this country after the war. That should be done not for the benefit of the companies themselves but so as to prevent them having to " go through the wringer," as they have had to do in days gone by; and more especially so that they may be in a position to give employment in times when employment may be sadly needed. Their resources should not be sapped too much. If you take away from them all their earnings in good times and give no consideration to the losses in bad times which most of them have experienced, some of these companies are going to find themselves, let us say, with expensive inventories at the expiration of this war. All the foresight in the world will not prevent some of them from having large and costly inventories on hand, and they may find that the value of their assets has shrunk overnight while their liabilities remain just the same. They may not be able to meet their obligations to their creditors, with the result that reorganizations are bound to follow.
What does that mean to the country? It means unemployment, reduced wages and generally bad times. I want to convey to the minister the idea of the need for broad vision; that these companies should not be taxed to death but should be put in a position to weather the next storm.

What about the
farmer?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Yes, I
agree, but at the moment I am not dealing with the farmer. These big companies provide the backbone of our employment in certain parts of eastern Canada-in my province, to a lesser degree in the minister's own province, and to a very large extent in Ontario and Quebec.
I do not want anybody to say that I am championing the bondholders of these companies. I know that thought will immediately arise in the minds of some. I have even heard it said that the whole basis of the Rowell-Sirois report is to protect the bondholders of the provinces at the expense of the dominion. I never thought that was the genesis of the report, and I do not think so yet; but there are people who will say it, and the minister will hear it before this session is over. That theory does not carry conviction to me. But the principle I am trying to

War Exchange Conservation Act
impress upon the minister is that these companies should be left reasonably sound in order to be able to weather the storms that may come. Revenue must be obtained, but let us take it from the ultimate recipients of the earnings of these companies. The principle followed in England is sound. We may have gone too far to go back to it now, but I do beg of the minister that he give consideration to what I know is a constructive suggestion with respect to company taxation and finance. Because after all, with the system of modern finance, these companies are the backbone of [DOT] industrial employment in Canada, and if they are not prosperous how can they give employment in bad times?
The minister has indicated the general trend of his ideas; he is going to make these allowances with respect to depreciation and depletion in return for certain undertakings to increase exports. The idea has a good deal of merit. I would like to have the principle developed a little further, and if he could be a little more definite it might be helpful in passing this resolution.
May I call the minister's attention to another consideration with respect to export trade and the increase in the volume of our United States exchange resulting therefrom. There is still in this country a substantial industry known as the lumber business, which for generation after generation was the backbone of the industrial life of the maritime provinces and eastern Canada, as I believe it is to-day of the industrial life of British Columbia. Is the minister prepared to say that consideration will be given to lumber companies which are not in the pulp and paper business but want to do an export trade, who have to suffer in a lesser degree in connection with the question of depreciation and depletion but will make a valuable contribution to the total import of United States dollars into Canada? I have an idea that our lumber men may be able to export a good deal more to the United States in coming days, especially if certain things happen, if the tempo of business is increased by certain eventualities in the United States which perhaps all of us are thinking about. Will the minister give consideration to extending this principle, rather nebulous yet, to export companies of that type, and not confine it so much to the bigger companies?-because I think it should go down the line. The line has to be drawn somewhere, but consideration might be given to all classes of business that are in the export trade in a reasonably large way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are included. There is no exclusion of lumber companies, or any kind of company for that matter.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am
just calling the minister's attention to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am anxious to get ahead, but let me say a word in respect to what the leader of the opposition says about taxation of companies. I am interested in hearing him take that stand, because hon. members cannot take two different stands-I am not talking about the hon. gentleman particularly. The feeling of this house last year certainly was that business interests were not to be allowed to use the war or the war period as a means of making profits in excess of ordinary normal profits. Now a doctrine has arisen-it may be a good one; I am not prepared to condemn it now. but it is certainly contrary to the former one. We find it in the financial press; to-day we hear it from the lips of the leader of the opposition. The sentiments he now expresses are very different from his stand last spring, when he was in favour of taking away from these companies all the excess profits that they earned during the war. If we are going to do that we cannot put them in a position to build up reserves against undefined losses in the future.
With regard to inventory reserves, the hon. gentleman referred to the probability that their inventories would suddenly drop in value at the end of the war. That was the experience at the end of the last war, and for that reason we embodied in the Excess Profits Tax Act a section providing, within certain carefully thought-out and defined limits, for inventory reserves. I do not see how we can possibly provide for general reserves against loss of profits due to some undefined circumstances that may arise in the post-war period. That would be equivalent to enabling them to prosper during the war, something to which the house was certainly opposed last session and to which I think it is still opposed.
There may be some middle ground. I pleaded for moderation last spring in this house; I said that in view of the fact that a great deal of our capital in this country had come from outside, and that a great many of our own people would do better if some profit incentive were left, I pleaded for moderation in this regard, and we were confronted by our friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation who said. "No, take it all away from them." And my hon. friend, and many of the members of his party, joined them. What has happened is exactly what I expected would happen. I knew that at every session we would have more and more members who, having in mind the experience of certain companies, perhaps companies in their own districts, would say, "Be a little easier on those

War Exchange Conservation Act
companies." Now, I am prepared to listen to all requests of companies, but I am not prepared to abandon the principle we laid down at the beginning, namely that companies during this war period shall not be allowed to strengthen or buttress their positions, or to build up reserves and make themselves prosperous, thinking that later there may be a loss of prosperity.

The minister made one very interesting admission, if I may say so, during the course of his remarks, namely, that the incentive which must be provided for industrial expansion is some additional profit. I want to draw the attention of the committee to that statement. We are appealing to our people to make sacrifices in a war period, yet the minister tells us that the government cannot take excess profits to the extent I believe they ought to be taken, because if that were done we should be providing no further incentive. Therefore the required incentive must be the incentive of profit, for that is what makes the wheels of industry go round.
In order perhaps to provide a little balance, the leader of the opposition having spoken as he did, I would say that we disagree with the point of view he has expressed. We object, too, to the powers given to the government under this proposal, whereby they may interfere with the excess profits tax. The house agreed this summer-members of this group dissenting-that the profits over and above the base period should be taxed at the rate of seventy-five per cent of the excess profit. That still left twenty-five per cent of the excess to the company.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Just to keep the record
straight: That, combined with the Income War Tax Act, left only 20-5 per cent. The combination of the two amounted to 79-5 per cent.

I am dealing with the excess profits tax, and the minister is bringing in some other tax. But we have left the companies with 20-5 per cent of the excess profits after excess and other taxes have been paid, an amount which, to my mind, is a considerable increase over what they had before.
I repeat now what we said in the summer, namely that to my mind the base is not equitable for the imposition of that tax. If we examine the records of some companies we shall find they made profits in 1939 as high as forty per cent, and their average would be around that for several years before. I would refer at this time to companies such as the Consolidated Mining and Smelting company, or Canadian Industries Limited.
Yet the proposal is that these plants shall be allowed to retain, if the government so permits, a percentage of the excess profits larger than that now allowed. I wish to register a most emphatic protest against the adoption of such a policy.
At the present time the gold mining industry is relieved from several forms of taxation. The ground given is that we require the gold. Of course, under existing circumstances, we require the gold in order that we may obtain the necessary dollar exchange in the United States. But in my opinion the necessities of this country, arising out of war effort, ought not to be the excuse for allowing corporations to escape taxation.
The other evening the minister said that the group to which I belong want to take over and to socialize all industry. That is not so.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Pretty
nearly.

No, it is not. We would take over at this time the industries essential to the carrying out of our war effort. We would take over the munitions industry, and if necessary the mining industry, and any others-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: And the banks.
-essential to our war effort.
And the paper industry?

At the present time that industry is not essential to our war effort. I believe that by progressive steps this nation, and other nations too, will take out of private hands and operate for the good of the community those industries which to-day are private, profit-making monopolies. Indeed, as I have often said, and as I shall repeat this afternoon, we believe that more people should own more property and that a few people should own a great deal less property than they now own. That is the basis of our plea. Whether we like it or not, it is coming, and coming fast.
One of the factors which will bring this condition about more quickly than any other is the type of class legislation implied in this particular item. I protest against it on behalf of the group with which I am associated. I protest, because I believe when we are calling upon our men to relinquish their homes, their jobs and everything else, we have the right to ask these industries to do without the profit motive or profit incentive.

War Exchange Conservation Act
Last night the minister gave the hon. member for Weyburn something in the nature of a verbal castigation because that hon. member had suggested that there were people in the country who were looking for profits and who ought to be controlled. Now we find, on the minister's own statement, that there are industries in Canada that we cannot expect to operate unless they show increased profits during war time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No, that is not a fair statement.

Yes, it is a fair statement; and if the leader of the opposition and the minister will read Hansard to-morrow they will find that that is the effect of the statement made in committee this afternoon- namely, that they want a further incentive.
Let me proceed to the next thought in that connection. We are told that we must put those industries in a position whereby they may give after-war employment. But our experience in the past has been that there was no employment unless industry could see a profit.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is not right.

That certainly is not
right.
It is true.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Half the paper companies in Canada-
I have the floor.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Then may I ask a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does the hon. member know that half the paper companies in Canada operated for years at a loss?

For thirteen
years.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
For at
least ten years some of them operated at a loss, but they continued to give employment.

That may be true, but it does not affect the argument I am making, namely that unless industry can see the prospect-I shall use that word-of a profit, there will be no industry, and the industry that can show a profit will be the one which will be operated. All one has to do is to look at our own economy to know that that is true. Industries such as those owned by distillery and liquor interests operated continuously because they could obtain money and make a profit fMr. Cold well.]
while other industries which might have given work and essential services to our 'people were idle.

Does the hon. member
know of any essential industry which is closed because of inability to make a profit?

A number of essential
industries were shut down or on part time during the depression.
This is war time.

In some cases they
were closed for days and weeks. Take the mining industry, for example. I know of mines that were closed down when people in the province in which I live were without coal. The need for the coal was there, but there was no profit because the people had no purchasing power and consequently the industry would not make deliveries.
A few days ago I asked for a return from the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe). I was anxious to obtain some information regarding new plants being built. I find that a great deal of the information which I require in order to understand what is going on has not been given because it is not considered to be in the public interest to give it. The government should tell the exact basis upon which plant extensions in private industry are being made. Many plants are being built and extended by the governments of Canada and Great Britain, and. if I understand the matter aright, there is a similar proposal involved in this.
If my information is correct, the rate of depreciation being allowed in privately-owned plants is such as these publicly-financed extensions can be written off in five years. My information may not be correct, and I have asked questions in order to get the correct information. If what I have just said is incorrect, then I want it corrected so that I may know precisely what is going on in the department. I want to protest against this method of making special allowances for depreciation or depletion to corporations under the Income War Tax Act and the Excess Profits Tax Act, if, in the opinion of the governor in council, such assistance is necessary in order that an expansion of the exports of any individual, partnership or corporation receiving such assistance may take place. That covers a great deal of ground, and in my opinion we are giving a very dangerous power to the government in providing that this type of assistance may be given to industry.

I think the hon. member
has missed the important point of this resolution. The purpose of the resolution is to increase Canada's exchange. I cannot conceive

War Exchange Conservation Act
of a healthy business without profit. It may be that the government will take that profit to carry on the war, but that is another matter entirely. Let us consider the individual. The profit that an individual makes is what he lives on.
Oh, no.

The profit that an individual in business makes is what he lives on. If he has a loss, he will have nothing to live upon. In the case of a corporation, the officials are paid before the profit is computed and there is a slightly different situation. I do not think this resolution is framed for the rich or large companies. I can see in it possibilities for the fishermen in my riding. The herring and mackerel fishermen in the maritime provinces can catch fish, but the prices on the foreign markets are so low that they have no profit. If certain expenses can be eliminated, then these men can ship their product to foreign countries and we will have the advantage of the exchange. I have in mind the vinegated herring industry, or herring cured in vinegar. There are fishermen and dealers in my riding who operate in a small way but who produce thousands of barrels of these vinegated herrings. This product has a ready market in the western states but at present the price is not sufficient to make a profit possible. Surely it would be in the interests of the country to have this industry stimulated.
Then in connection with the newsprint and pulp industry, it seems to me that if this industry can increase its production it would bring more exchange to the country. At the present time no newsprint or pulp is coming in from Europe. Surely abnormal extension expenditures could be written off in a way that would not prove a burden when we return to normal times. I think this would be eminently in the interests of the people of the country. To make this resolution the subject of an attack on the capitalistic system is not in keeping with our war effort. The capitalistic system is not perfect; it was conceived by man and anything conceived by man is not perfect. But for the last hundred years it has been the best way devised for the orderly progress of society, and until I can see something better-I am always looking for something better-I am not prepared to step into some unknown which will reduce this country to a condition similar to that prevailing in the countries of Europe where the conflict is going on at the present time.

Last evening the minister said that if hon. members opposite to him were able to see some deep meaning in this legislation which he could not see, he 14873-48
wished they would tell him. This resolution provides for assistance to individuals, partnerships or corporations by way of tax credits or special allowances for depreciation or depletion. There are individuals, partnerships or corporations which have invested United States funds in this country to develop our natural resources. If in due time they have dividends to disburse and ask the foreign exchange control board for United States exchange, then I suggest to the minister that should any of these individuals, partnerships or corporations appeal for assistance under this section they should be told either to pay their dividends in Canadian funds or to refrain from going to the foreign exchange control board for United States funds with which to pay dividends.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member is referring to United States owned companies.

I tried to make that abundantly clear last night. I have one other suggestion to make, apart altogether from this one, but having to do with the conservation of foreign exchange. Many United States owned companies make interplant shipments from Canada to the United States which are invoiced at prices far below the true market value. It is difficult to establish this, but these prices should be checked in the United States in order to make sure that we are getting the full United States exchange for these exports. Some commodities are shipped to the United States for further processing before being marketed. I have one firm in mind which placed $100,000 in their depreciation reserves for the day when commodity prices might drop considerably. When any of these individuals, partnerships or corporations appeal for concessions under this resolution I hope the department will see to it that they invoice shipments from their Canadian to their United States plants at the full market value in order that Canada may obtain the full exchange value of the shipment. I just throw that out as a suggestion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think the income tax
division takes some pains to see that that is done.
Mr. O'BRIEN: Mr. Chairman, so far I have remained almost mute in the deliberations of the house, and it is not my desire now to delay the committee. I find this discussion very interesting for the reason that as I am in business, as most of the members are, it is something that we can put our teeth into. The war discussion has been so abstract at times that I have felt bewildered.
During this discussion the word "incentive" has been mentioned, and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) has voiced a view



War Exchange Conservation Act
which I should like to commend. The immediate incentive is not altogether the point, but, it seems to me, as he so ably suggested, that the future is a very important item to consider.	.
Coming as I do from the county of Northumberland, which depends almost entirely on the lumbering business, as do also the constituencies of Gloucester, Restigouche-Mada-waska, Victoria-Carleton, York, Kent, and virtually all the northern counties of New Brunswick, I know that this item is a matter of vital importance to our province and particularly to what I might term the owner-managed type of business. Some reference has been made to-day to corporations. Corporations I think are usually able to take care of themselves, but the smaller owner-managed type of business usually suffers owing to the fact that there is no organization in which their difficulties can be discussed with a view to getting relief. For that reason I wish to compliment the minister upon the degree of flexibility which is being achieved, because, as we all know, in times like the present there must of necessity be generally speaking, rigid control.
When a government or a department is dealing with matters of business, certainly business principles should be followed; for any business, to be successful, must of necessity have a great degree of flexibility in its structure. Therefore I am happy to note with reference to individuals, partnerships or corporations that each situation may be flexibly treated on its merits. That I think is a splendid thing.
Referring to the Ottawa Journal of this morning, to which the leader of the opposition also referred, it seems to me that the report as to government aid to the newsprint industry is a bit premature because that is what we are attempting to determine here at the moment. But if it should be the decision of this committee that aid should be given to the newsprint industry, and the department is given the necessary authority, I suggest that if relief is given, and I am in favour of the principle in the circumstances-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No relief is to be given
to the newsprint industry, but the same concession will be available to them if they can produce exchange as a result of the concession. But the idea is not to relieve the companies.
Mr. O'BRIEN: Concession or relief.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Before any return is made they must do thus and so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes.

Mr. O'BRIEN: I would hope that we might follow along the same line in connection with the primary producer, the producer of pulpwood, for instance. I am not going to quote any figures here to-day because frankly I believe business should be smart enough to govern its own affairs and create its own destiny so that government would not be forced to interfere and control business.
Whether it be done by statute or by persuasion, and I much prefer persuasion, it seems to me that the newsprint industry should be informed that the primary producer of pulp-wood, the farmer, is not receiving a sufficient return in view of the increased profits and the much greater returns which evidently the newsprint companies are making to-day. I am informed that pulpwood in Nova Scotia-it may be so-called distress wood-is now being sold at $7 a cord, which I think is a price unfairly low. Whether the matter should be looked after by the war-time prices and trade board or by some other agency I do not know, but on October 29 I wrote the Canadian Pulp and Paper association drawing attention to the matter and stating my belief that the pulp and paper industry should consider it. I received a non-committal reply, almost a month later. I hope the pulp and paper business will be smart enough to realize that if this adjustment is not made voluntarily by the business itself it will eventually be done through government control.
There is another matter in connection with the small lumber business, to which I should like to refer. I wrote to the minister with regard to this and received a friendly and I think useful reply, stating that he would be glad to have any suggestions. In the lumber business as carried on in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, the operations take place in small portable mills, which do not permit of any large capital investment; consequently depreciation on the plants used by these small owner-managed businesses is practically nil. I am convinced that those of us engaged in the lumber business in the maritime provinces wish to carry on that business in order to supply the necessary material required for Great Britain's war effort. We are not particularly anxious to make enormous profits. But as the leader of the opposition has suggested, provision should be made so that in the future some reserve may be allowed. That is perhaps looking too far ahead, but I have been wondering if it would not be possible to devise some scheme along this line. Let us say that a company pay a $5,000 tax-I am speaking of an owner-managed business. In return a certificate might be given to them for a certain portion of that tax to be re-issued

War Exchange Conservation Act
without interest to the person making the payment, so that in future years, when war business ceases and unemployment and depression are perhaps again our unhappy lot, the certificate might be taken by the lumber operator or the operator of any other line of business to his bank as security. Some future generation might thus reimburse the present day operators in view of the severe war conditions they have to contend with to-day. As a matter of fact I think such a certificate of the dominion would be as valuable to the bank as some types of bonds. I hope that when these concessions are being arranged-because I appreciate the necessity for creating exchange-some consideration will be given to the primary producer, particularly the small farmer pulp-wood producer.

Mr. Chairman, I rose for the purpose of asking a question of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) but he has left the house so I shall have to leave that till later. Somebody had asked him whether he would consider farming an essential industry to be taken over by the government.
Surely the hon. member does not think that farming is a monopoly.

I was talking not about monopolies but about industries. I should like to ask the minister if this section we are now dealing with is wide enough to enable the government to make whatever arrangements might be deemed desirable to assist coal. I have in mind particularly Alberta, where coal is a vital matter to us. My information is that about $93,000,000 went to the United States last year for the purchase of coal by Canadians. It seems to me that this is a very important question, much more important, in fact, as regards the conservation of exchange than the matters with which we have been dealing, although I do not quarrel with those at all. Is this section which we are dealing with wide enough to promote a greater market for Canadian coal in the way of subventions or lower freight rates or in any similar manner?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. This measure does not affect industries which rely on the domestic market. This is to encourage export industries for the purpose of obtaining exchange.

As I understand it, the
purpose of this resolution is to help increase Canada's supply of foreign exchange. That is being done by giving certain remissions of taxation in order to expand exports.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: The discussion to-day has taken the form of considering exports to the United States. In British Columbia practically all the lumber which is exported goes either to Great Britain or to one of the empire countries, in which transactions, of course, there is no such thing as United States exchange. Is it the intention that this power shall be used to assist the lumber industry to expand its exports to British empire countries?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, that is not the intention of the legislation. Although it is possible under this bill, it is not considered desirable to limit the powers so as to make that entirely impossible. But it is not my intention at the moment to recommend assistance except for the single purpose of increasing our supplies of par currency exchange.

Last evening the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) raised the question of promoting the production of silver. Frankly, I thought he made an excellent presentation. I believe that many of us in this house are in entire agreement with the stand he took. But the minister did not answer the hon. member's question. I would ask him to tell us the attitude of the government with regard to encouraging the production of silver so that it may be exported to the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
An application from the
silver mining industry for assistance under this measure would be considered. If the industry is exporting silver and feels that it could obtain exchange for this country by increasing, with assistance, its exports, it would be possible within the letter and spirit of the proposed legislation for the government te assist it. Whether that would be economically desirable I am not prepared to say; it might or it might not. It would depend upon the facts.

That does not quite answer
the question. The proposition made last night was that the government give consideration to doing the same with regard to silver as we are doing with regard to gold, so as to lend encouragement to operators of silver mines, to give employment in Canada, and to provide Canadian dollars in the United States. The answer given just now by the minister in reply to the hon. member for Vancouver South is not exactly in keeping with the argument which I advanced last night.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know. I will consider it, if the hon. member will write me outlining the respects in which he wants consideration to be given. The hon. member has a third of which I am not aware, and if he will write to me I will consider it.

I am wondering
whether or not the minister has considered the implications of this type of legislation. I protested against this last evening, and I am going to repeat my protest, because I think it applies even more to this type of legislation than to that which I objected to last evening. This amounts in effect to parliament granting to the governor in council the right to interpret statutes according to the needs of foreign exchange at the moment. Under the provisions of the war tax act and the Excess Profits Tax Act, statutory provision is made for the deductions that can be made for depreciation and so on; and what in effect parliament will do if it allows this resolution to pass is to give approval to the dangerous proposition that statutes shall be on the statute books but may be applied in such way as the governor in council may consider advisable in the interests of foreign exchange. That is what it does.
If the war tax act is not sufficient, amend it. If the Excess Profits Tax Act goes too far, and I am not arguing that at the moment, why should not the government take it upon itself to amend it? This resolution in effect allows the governor in council to relieve any individual or company from the law of the

land, and I think this is a most serious matter. Surely there must be one law for all individuals and companies in this land. We have now come to the position where the government says, "We are going to leave on the statute book these statutes, the war tax act and the Excess Profits Tax Act, but we are going to make such orders in council as we deem necessary from time to time to relieve certain individuals, persons or companies from the application of the law of the land as set out therein."
I repeat my protest against this kind of legislation. I submit that its passage will create a dangerous precedent. It will destroy the rule of law. I realize that in time of war our people must give up some rights in the greater interests of the safety of the state, but I emphatically protest against legislation of this type, which will permit the executive to create inequalities under law in this nation. It allows the governor in council to say to one individual or company, "You shall operate under the law of the land," and to another individual or company, "You are to be relieved from operating under the law of the land." My submission is that this is a most dangerous principle, because the essence of law, whether in war or in peace, must be uniformity, certainty of application and reasonable definiteness. If we pass this type of legislation empowering the executive to enforce the law for one individual or company and relieve another from its application, we destroy the rule of law. We permit the law to be elastically applied and give to the executive power such as has never been asked of this house, nor, do I believe, of any other parliament.
Last night in reference to this very matter I asked why this type of legislation was being brought up, and the minister answered: "We had the power to act under the War Measures Act, because if ever there was a war measure this is one. We did not think, however, that that would be acting in the true spirit of the constitution. We thought that when parliament was here we ought to lay the matter before parliament and state what we intended to do." The minister nods agreement with that statement. "Does the minister contend that under the War Measures Act the executive of this nation had the right to say to one individual, "You shall pay the tax provided by the Excess Profits Tax Act," and to another individual, "You are relieved from it"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

The minister says, yes. I do not think the courts of the land

That is quite a
different thing.

It is a different
principle, I submit. These are statutes which make certain provisions that apply to every person in the country, and what the government is now asking is that it shall have the power to relieve certain persons from the law to a greater or lesser extent. Against that type of legislation I protest.

I warmly support what has just been said by the hon. member (Mr. Diefenbaker). It seems to me we are in danger of placing on the statute book provisions which become more or less windowdressing, because people do believe that taxes are to be imposed as laid down by parliament in the budget of last summer. If we give the power implied in the government's resolution we have nothing but dead letters which deceive a good many people. I believe that the point made by the hon. member has been well taken.
I was out for four or five minutes just now and I understand a question was asked by the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Casselman). I should like to answer it. As I understand it, the question was whether I considered that farms should be subject to socialization by the state. My answer is, no. To-day farmers are being squeezed by the monopolies of which I have spoken. We believe that when an institution exploits society so that it becomes a matter for the protection of society, it should be taken over. The farmer, the producer, never makes a profit in the sense in which I have used the term profit, which is the residue left after
all other costs including depreciation have been met. It is consequently a reward unearned which goes entirely to the ownership of capital.
Was it only to monopolies the hon. member was directing his remarks?
Monopolistic industries.

I take exception to this section 6. Last summer when the excess profits tax was imposed, the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) suggested that these mining corporations were already enjoying enviable profits. The Excess Profits Tax Act, according to the minister, allows them 20 per cent in excess of what they have enjoyed in the last few years. In view of the fact that we are appealing to all groups in Canada to make the fullest contribution to the war effort, I submit that the admission by the minister that there is some difficulty in getting some of these corporations to play their full part should warrant the government in carrying out the provision made under the National Resources Mobilization Act, section 2 of which provides:
Subject to the provisions of section three hereof, the governor in council may do and authorize such acts and things, and make from time to time such orders and regulations, requiring persons to place themselves, their services and their property at the disposal of His Majesty in the right of Canada, as may be deemed necessary or expedient for securing the public safety, the defence of Canada, the maintenance of public order, or the efficient prosecution of the war, or for maintaining supplies or services essential to the life of the community.
If any difficulty is being experienced in getting the necessary foreign exchange the government should at once take action under the act. I strongly object to giving the government the wide powers asked for in section 6.
