Before this resolution passes may I make two or three comments? In the first place I wish to associate myself with the minister in his observation regarding profits, and in his endeavour to manage matters so that industry can make a profit. It is to this question of profit that I wish to refer.
In the first place the minister, without knowing it, has begun, in these provisions to assure a fair profit, to move in the direction of social credit in respect of the just price. I am afraid that statement may not appeal to him, but after a while it will not look nearly so bad. I believe that before the war is over, before production is at the peak at which we all want it to be, the minister will have to go a great deal further than he has gone already. Either he or the Minister of Munitions and Supply has already gone a long way in another direction-that of advancing money to assist in the establishment of distinctive war industries. Let us take as an illustration-I have no other in mind at the moment-the ammonia plant which I understand is to be established in Alberta. If the government were unable to find a company that dared to risk its capital in the construction of an ammonia plant, they might say to the people concerned: Look here, we realize that the war may end in a year or two, and that if you put your money in this plant you may lose it; we are therefore prepared to help you bear the burden. We are ready to- assume a certain amount of the risk; we will advance from government funds say half the total amount necessary for your capital expenditure.
Now, that is completely sound. It is some-tiling which has been done, is being done and will be done to a greater and greater extent before the war is over. What the government have undertaken to do there is to make productive loans. At the present time the government is either collecting that money from the people in the form of taxation, or borrowing it. But I contend very seriously that after a .(Mr. R. B. Hanson.]
while it will come to be seen quite clearly that the money might just as well be created. If the money can be spent when it is borrowed, or when it is taxed, without causing inflation, it can be spent when it is created without causing inflation. This is an extremely important matter, which I think has not yet become clarified in people's thinking. But men are making good progress. I have a passage here from a speech by Mr. G. W. Spinney-I suppose he would have a nightmare if he knew I was referring to him in support of social credit-before the shareholders of the Bank of Montreal on December 3, in which he made a remark which shows a great advance towards modern concepts of money.
Having used this illustration, may I point out that the minister is pursuing a perfectly sound principle in advancing money free of interest as a loan, as a gift to a producer who is going to bring into being commodities which the government or the people will sorely need. I believe that the informed thinking people in Canada will support the minister in doing that. Common sense would say that if we need ammonia, let us have ammonia, and if we have to give the money to a company to get the ammonia, let us do it. That is sound thinking, as I think the ordinary person will agree.
The minister can go still further. He can arrange to allow the company that is producing the ammonia to buy its raw materials at a reduced price brought about by a direct payment by the government of part of the price of the goods being used by the company. I do not know just what is used in the production of ammonia, but if, for example, it were zinc, the government could arrange to see that the company got its zinc at, say, ten per cent below the market price.
I am sorry to be taking so much time, but the discussion has been extremely interesting and valuable; I have not thus far taken up much of the time of the committee, and I believe I have a message that is important in relation to the matter under consideration.
I was speaking of a discount on the price of raw material. Or the government might say: We will remit part of the cost by paying part of the freight rate on the raw material. That again would be of direct assistance to the company and an assurance that they would make a profit. Or the government might go further and remit the sales tax on .the raw-material in order to enable the company to sell its product at greater advantage.
All these matters are devices which are in the minds of social crediters as possible means of helping producers produce. As I said the other day, there is no nonsense to it; it is

War Exchange Conservation Act
just common sense in action, as will be clearly seen by anyone who takes the time to examine these proposals calmly and dispassionately and without prejudice.
I turn to the matter of conserving exchange. It is clear that the government should advance money to help produce ammonia, say, but it has perhaps not become clear that the government can afford to advance money to producers of other things, say wool, or shoes, which happen to be needed. If the government carry this process far enough to assist in the production of shoes, for example, they will enable the people who are producing shoes in Canada to produce and sell at such a low rate that people will buy Canadian shoes instead of shoes from the United States. They will prevent the importation of shoes made in the United States, and thereby conserve exchange.
Let me turn for a moment to the remark of the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Casselman) the other night. I believe I was just a little discourteous to him-

Will the hon. member
tell us how many shoes are imported from
the United States?

Well, if shoes are
an unfortunate example, let us take something else. If the hon. member is asking a sincere question, very well; but if he is asking it just to interrupt me, it is another matter. Suppose we are importing carrots. If the government advanced money to help someone in Canada build a greenhouse in which to produce carrots so as to supply our winter market, the principle would be the same; it would prevent the importation of carrots and other vegetables from the United States and thereby conserve exchange. Once this idea is apprehended by the people we shall approach from an entirely different angle the matter of conserving foreign exchange.

What would happen to
the Canadian farmer if the United States did the same in respect to our cattle? We manufacture between ninety-seven and ninety-eight per cent of all our shoes.

The hon. member is asking a very good question but he is confused by the anomalies of our present system. He cannot tell to save his life what to do with the various commodities of which we now have a surplus, such as the wheat that the farmer of western Canada is producing in abundance. He raises these questions which confront us under our present system, whereby the country is cluttered up from end to end with unsalable products-in itself an indication that it is essential to have a change in the
system. We could eliminate the consumption of foreign goods just as Canada could eliminate the buying of United States steel if the production of Canadian iron were promoted and our dependence on United States iron done away with. We can in large measure eliminate the need for United States exchange without raising any difficulties or doing anything which might be objectionable. We can also gradually increase our own production, thereby avoiding inflation; we can increase our home consumption, which will raise the standard of living among the people, make for prosperity and happiness, and give the government a greater taxing base, which is another thing much to be desired.
What I am about to say now may not appear to bear directly on the question under discussion, but certainly it does relate to it indirectly. If the adjusting is done with created money instead of with borrowed or taxed money, the strain on the Canadian people will be removed. The only question which arises is whether such action will cause inflation. Again let me say that if we can borrow money which would not ordinarily be spent, and spend it without causing a rise in prices, we can create the same amount of money and spend it without giving rise to inflation. I believe that is quite clear.
If we create the money we will avoid inflation provided that we take care to look for four things. First, we must see to it that we have plenty of goods; second, we must have a sufficient variety of those goods; third, we must have plenty of resources to produce more goods, and, fourth, we must have the planning which will supply a still greater variety and a greater abundance.
For example, let us consider the facts in connection with wool. We may have the fear that if we permit money to go into circulation the price of wool will go up. But if we produce more wool we shall have then approached the matter from an entirely different angle. We could increase the wool production of Canada to such an extent that the Canadian people could not begin to buy all the Canadian wool, and endanger a rise in price. Once the government approaches the problem from that angle it will have an altogether different outlook concerning the whole inflation situation, and will understand what I said the other day-that it is following a niggardly policy with respect to Canada. It is starving the Canadian people down, instead of stimulating them to the greatest possible production and to consumption which will give them the greatest possible strength in the contest upon which we have only entered.
I shall now turn to the matter of profits. As the hon. member for Edmonton East will

War Exchange Conservation Act
probably see, by following the proposals I was making the other day when I said we were living in an age of plenty, he would see that we would have plenty of foreign exchange if we had plenty of production of a sufficiently great variety at a sufficiently low price. So that the problem would be cleared up.
Provided you could get the other country to buy your goods.
Yes, but if you could not get the other country to buy your goods you would have accomplished one great thing when you produced plenty and enabled your own people to buy them.
What about the production of more wheat?

I shall come to that. That is one of the things confounding people to-day; Canadians do not see how to deal with it. Before I finish my speech I wish to deal with it, although it is not part of the subject of the debate. If the hon. member wishes to ask questions when I have finished my observations I shall be only too pleased to answer them, because I am not advocating anything that is not scientifically sound.
Social credit is simply a new order, that is all. It is a way by which we can raise revenue without dragging ourselves down into a state of niggardly scarcity, through which we are in danger of being defeated.
This question may be raised: Why did the Social Credit party support the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in their attitude toward the taking away of money from people who had money to spare? I would draw the attention of the house to the fact that the amendment then under consideration said, in effect, "We will take a compulsory war loan, free of interest, according to ability to subscribe-"

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry, but the hon. member cannot refer to another debate of the same session.

I bow to your ruling, and shall not continue along that line.
I agree with the minister when he says that under the present system it is necessary that companies must have a profit. There is no possibility of avoiding it, and there are several reasons why. Companies need to have a profit because, as has been pointed out, they are afraid of the aftermath of the war. When a man invests $100,000 in a plant, knowing that almost any day the war may come to an end and his market may be lost and his investment thereby jeopardized, he will of course require a sufficient profit.

Canada could organize on such a basis that producers would not demand exorbitant profits. If there were an arrangement whereby we could guarantee to the farmer that no more wheat would be produced than could be used, he would not be taking such a tremendous risk if he were to invest $10,000 in a farm. The same reasoning is true with respect to a company. If we could guarantee that production and consumption would be planned and that prices would be maintained at stable levels, with no fear of disastrous changes in tariff or of loss of trade as a result of which a man might be ruined, there would be no necessity for all these great profits which companies are now so eagerly trying to get.
In my view, under the capitalistic system, the profit motive is quite sound. The hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Kinley) spoke wisely: without profits we simply cannot get along under the capitalistic system. The minute we try to do so, production is stopped. The only way to induce production would then be by threat of punishment. If that were done we would have regimentation.
We want profit, but we do not want exploitation. I do not think my hon. friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation would object to profit so long as there were no exploitation.
Don't offer them any; they won't refuse it.

I think that is probably so. Perhaps my ideas are somewhat at variance with those of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar when it comes to a discussion of profits. But man has not yet found any effective incentive for production other than that of profit. It is dangerous to seek to abolish the profit motive. I believe the minister has realized that fact, and as a result he is now introducing these measures.
It is part of our lives.

Yes, I would say it is. We must take the choice between profit and regimentation-and I do not for one moment favour regimentation. It is said that Lenin brought in the machine gun to take the place of the profit motive. Well, that was not a good thing; it immediately brought about a dictatorship. I believe you can encourage people to produce all you want them to produce. You can encourage them to sell at whatever price you wish to prevail, if you just manage the profit properly. The profit motive is the only way of preserving democracy, because the very minute you force a man to raise wheat or to work, for example, in a mine, you have destroyed completely democracy.

War Exchange Conservation Act
I believe we must contrive to give a fair profit, or one adequate to encourage production; there must be a profit for all- for primary as well as for secondary producers, for farmer as well as manufacturer.
May I turn once more to the observations of the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg. As I understand the situation, there are two distinct classes of production. First there is the primary producer, such as the fisherman or the farmer, who, generally speaking, lives on his profit. But the man engaged in, we will say, machine manufacturing, does not necessarily live on his profit. His wages or his living are included in the cost which goes into the price of his output.
If he operates as an incorporated company.
Yes.
He creates another person, in law, to carry on his business.

Yes. We must bear in mind the fact that the farmer simply cannot live without profit, because that is all the living he has. How can the fisherman live without profit? He must make money. We must distinguish between the profit of the primary producer who lives on his profit, and the profit of the secondary producer who does not live on his profit. But the secondary producer uses his profit to pad and to protect himself against eventualities to come. Therefore he needs profit-in fact a rather large profit. Once we get that in our minds we can stop worrying about big profits and big industry. The iron industry is a war industry. The man conducting such a plant is constantly worrying over what he is going to do after the war is over. He is thinking of the day when iron will not be needed to kill men, when there will be a surplus of that commodity in the world. He wonders how he will be able to sell iron then.
What could happen was seen in the last war when sugar production was increased to such a tremendous extent that after the war there was more sugar than the people could use and the sugar producers were almost all ruined. The men who are conducting our war industries are certainly worrying about what is going to happen when they are not able to sell their products. The man engaged in war industry should be dealt with in a particular kind of way. He has his own money invested and there is the investment of his shareholders. These are the main reasons why he needs considerable profits. There should be a fair profit for both the primary and the secondary producer.
May I suggest once more that consideration be given to what is known as the social credit just price by the creation and wise use of money based upon the goods-and-services-producing-and-consuming-power of the country. For example, the amount of money which can be created and given to farmers in price modifications depends upon whether there are plenty of things that are used by the farmers which the farmers can buy with the money they earn. If there are, the money will not cause inflation. Again: The amount of money which can be created and advanced to railways as freight adjustments depends upon what commodities the railways will spend the money which they receive, and whether there are sufficient goods for which they can spend the money without causing a rise in prices. The railroads will buy coal. Is there plenty of coal? They will buy oil. Is there plenty of oil? If there is plenty of oil and plenty of coal, there will be no rise in the prices of those commodities. As soon as we begin to look at the matter in this way, the dread of social credit proposals will be removed immediately.
To sum up, I agree completely with the minister when he says that there must be a fair profit. Measures must also be taken to help the producers not only to produce all we want, but to produce it at prices that will give the producers, both primary and secondary, a return for their production.

It is to be regretted that in the dying minutes of this part of the session we should have to consider such important legislation as this is embodied in this resolution. We spent weeks and days in the last session discussing the budget and amending the Income War Tax Act and the Excess Profits Tax Act, but by this one resolution practically the whole thing is being wiped out in that it places within the power of the governor in council the right to discriminate and grant special privileges.

The trouble that I see in connection with this legislation is that it is bound to lead to some form of discrimination. An individual, partnership or corporation may be granted assistance by way of special tax credits or special allowances for depreciation or depletion under the Income War Tax Act. It seems to me that every company in Canada will be asking for this. These companies will be compelled to ask for favours from the administration, and I do not see how certain businesses can continue to exist in such an atmosphere. Already the government has taken certain representatives of big business into some of the departments, and it seems to me that the natural result of this legislation will be increased lobbying. There will be a disgraceful scramble for special concessions, and the successful lobbyists will be able to wipe out any opposition.

This creates a monopoly, and industries in less favoured parts of this dominion may suffer considerably. The resources of Canada are owned in a large part by monopolistic organizations. They own and control much of the machinery of production. Owning the natural resources of this country and having control of production, they are able to tell the primary producer what he shall get for the commodity he raises and can dictate to labour what it shall receive.
Will the hon. member name just one monopoly?
The oil industry and the power industry in eastern Canada.

We have the hydro
electric power commission in Ontario which is not a monopoly, but a public utility.
Beauharnois and Montreal Light, Heat and Power company.
Nickel is a world monopoly.

Also the General Electric Company of America. Many businesses can continue only upon the condition of their claims being favourably considered by government officials. I cannot see how justice can exist in such an atmosphere. I cannot see how we can continue to sit in this house and favourably consider legislation which will grant one kind of treatment to one group of people and give special privileges to another. It will be a sad day for the people of Canada if this thing should continue any further.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to speak at any length on this matter, but I wish to point out to the government that perhaps they should spend a little time in reading the remarks of the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore). If that were done-and I say this advisedly-then as far as I am concerned there would be no objection to this resolution passing. As it now stands, however, I am definitely opposed to it because in my opinion it is class legislation. I think the minister must acknowledge that this is just another belt-tightening process and it will be something that will bear most heavily upon the common people. There is to be an increased price for washing machines, but I do not think anyone ever bought a washing machine as a luxury. When you begin to increase the price on articles such as this, you just make it that much more difficult for the common people. This resolution reads:
That the governor in council in order to increase Canada's supply of foreign exchange-

War Exchange Conservation Act
There are many other ways of increasing our supply of foreign exchange, as the hon. member for Lethbridge pointed out.
-may, on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance, enter into agreements with individuals, partnerships or corporations-
I fancy that the minister has not in mind the agricultural or fishing industries, and I am sure that he has not in mind the fruit growers. If this is to be class legislation, then it is definitely wrong.
-to grant assistance by way of special tax credits and/or .special allowances for depreciation or depletion under the Income War Tax Act and the Excess Profits Tax Act-
There is a great danger in these depreciation allowances.
-if, in the opinion of the governor in council, such assistance is necessary in order that an expansion of the exports of any individual, partnership or corporation receiving such assistance may take place.
According to the minister himself, these large corporations are making an excess profit of 20-4 per cent, so that besides making their regular profit over the base period, and an additional 20-4 per cent, we are going to grant still further concessions to them. I really fear the outcome. This type of legislation is not going to stimulate patriotism; it is going to create dissatisfaction among those who joined the army because of economic insecurity, and it is not conducive to the creation of unity in Canada, which we so greatly need at this time.
We talk of equality of sacrifice and service. I am in favour of that principle, and I am convinced that if there were an indication to the public, even to the members here, that there was going to be equality of sacrifice and service for all classes and every part of Canada, such a step would do much to promote unity. But at a time when agriculture, fishing, and coal mining are not making the profit they did before; when many of the workers in those industries are still unemployed, and when the cost of living is going up for the common people, the government brings down legislation like this favouring the big industries still further. I recommend to the minister that he give close scrutiny to the speech which has just been made by the hon. member for Lethbridge.

The other day a question
arose as to the relative vitamin content of orange juice and tomato juice. In order to clarify the situation, so that there might be no mistake either in this house or among the Canadian people, I got in touch with Doctor

War Exchange Conservation Act
Tisdall in Toronto. I can now give the exact result of an investigation made in the laboratory of the department of paediatrics in the university of Toronto, which is under the direction of Doctor Alan Brown, who has associated with him an eminent nutrition expert, Doctor F. F. Tisdall. The result of their investigation will be found in the June, 1940, issue of the Canadian Hospital, in which is given the total vitamin C content-vitamin C I should explain is ascorbic acid-as determined by chemical means, of various fresh and canned juices which were bought at retail in Toronto during the winter of 1939-40. The ascorbic acid (vitamin C' content is given in milligrammes per 100 cubic centimetres and per ounce, together with the milligrammes of ascorbic acid purchasable for one cent.
The vitamin C or ascorbic acid content of citrus juice varies considerably in the different varieties. In the table given, the content of vitamin C in one ounce of canned California orange juice is 11*3 milligrammes. In the best brand of sieved canned tomato juice it is 6-9 milligrammes. It takes, therefore, only a little over one and a half times as much tomato juice to get the same amount of vitamin C as there is in California orange juice. It will therefore be seen that the statement made by an hon. member the other day that it would take twenty times as much tomato juice is not correct. The juice of sieved Canadian canned tomatoes is as economical a source of ascorbic acid or vitamin C as the juice obtained from fresh California oranges, and also as useful for health as grapefruit juice or any other citrus fruit juice.
I think it will only be necessary to call the attention of the Canadian public to this fact in order to have them make a much wider use of tomato juice than they are now making, and also to enable them as a war measure to discontinue the use of orange or grapefruit juice and substitute in its place a homegrown product which will not only be as healthful but also be of advantage by conserving foreign exchange.
Just to complete this statement, I should say that because it does require a slightly larger bulk, for very young infants grapefruit juice or orange juice would be preferable. But that will be only a very small part of the requirements of the country.

Would the minister explain generally what it is proposed to do in connection with petroleum products? The matter has been running through my mind because of the large consumption of gasoline in this country and the necessity of supplies in future. Another consideration which appeals to me is that we need to curtail as far as possible duplication of effort. Take, for example, a city like Toronto. We have a good streetcar service and a bus service as well, so that a great many people could very well dispense with driving their cars down-town. In certain instances, of course, people need

To-day motor buses compete with our own railroads, and altogether the consumption of gasoline is very large. I find from the "Canada Year Book" that our consumption in 1939 was 762,740,326 gallons, and refunds were allowed on 130,722,877 gallons, so that 632,017,449 gallons were used in motor cars and similar vehicles. I assume that the refunds represent the amount of gasoline used by farmers and essential to their requirements. speechtext:
That may be true. I think nobody can say arbitrarily just what the increase is. I believe that the minister has now made a fairer and truer statement of the position. In view of the increased cost of production on the other side, I do not think there will be in the immediate future any great influx of cotton goods into Canada. But it may be very valuable. I believe Lancashire knows that, because I saw some newspaper comments which appeared after the minister had delivered his speech, indicating that the cotton people of Lancashire were most profuse in their thanks. They were quite enthusiastic about this so-called let-down of the bars. It may work out that way.
At the moment I do not think there is any great danger, because -there are obstacles and impediments in the way. At the same time may I point out to the minister a few important factors. The cotton business in England has been rationalized, and cotton exports are being bonused by the association of cotton manufacturers in England. That is the information I have before me. The minister is letting in free this bonused production. That would seem to be the effect of the provision. No doubt the minister has expert factual information which is not available -to me, but I would ask him to give consideration to that phase of the matter. If that production is being bonused for export, then I suggest the position should be reexamined.
The second point to which I wish to call the minister's attention is this:	Canadian
cotton manufacturers have to pay a 10 per cent excise tax, as well as the ordinary foreign exchange premium on all cotton imported. But the British manufacturer does not have

War Exchange Conservation Act
to pay any such excise tax, and the result is that there is a 10 per cent increase in the cost of the raw material to the Canadian manufacturer. This would seem to be an unfair situation, and it should be compensated for by an excise tax on imported cotton goods or, as an alternative, on the cost of the raw cotton content thereof. That would balance the arrangement. In other words, there is a differential to the extent of that tax operating against the Canadian manufacturer. It would seem that our manufacturers are taxed in a way in which the British manufacturers are not taxed. The manufacturer in England will not have to pay the excise tax on his finished product. I suggest an examination should be made to see if he should not pay that 10 per cent tax on the value of the cotton content-not necessarily on the labour. I believe the condition I have described constitutes a serious handicap.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are various factors
to be considered. The British manufacturer has a greater exchange disadvantage.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I realize
that. I suggest, however, that if, upon examination, the officials in the minister's department find any injustice, a correction should be made. The officials now sitting in front of the minister will appreciate the point I have made.
I would point out to the minister that labour costs in Canada were 60 per cent higher than corresponding costs in Great Britain. I do not know just what the situation is at the present time. It is impossible to give the Canadian worker the standard of living to which we believe he or she is entitled, and at the same time meet the competition of the cheaper labour used in the manufacture of imported goods. The important consideration is that there is a difference in the prices paid to labour here and labour over there.
I should dislike very much to see any necessity for a reduction in our wage scale. I do not think our workers could stand it because, no matter what the minister may say, the cost of living is going up. The wholesale index indicates an increase, and costs of retail goods have increased. I believe they will continue, willy-nilly to go up. In my community the price of milk is increasing steadily, the price being fixed by the milk board. Because of the processing tax on flour, the price of flour is going up. I do not know whether wages are keeping pace with these increases. They will, however, have to. I do not anticipate any great difficulty in this matter at the present time, but these are factors which must be kept in mind. If there is any injustice, steps ought to be taken to make the necessary correction.
I have tried to place before the committee the three points I had in mind which, it ' seemed to me, were important factors. I am not opposing the resolution before the committee, but I am simply describing the situation as I understand it.

Will the minister not consider making reference in this section to parts I and II of schedule 1 ? We have had the bill in our hands for just a minute, but so far as I can see, there is no mention in it of parts I and II of schedule 1. That would appear to me to be rather loose draftsmanship. ,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I gave consideration to that last night, and there are reasons why I do not think it would be desirable. There will have to be some freedom to deal with even the items in part I. This is not ordinary tariff legislation; this is emergency import control. This is concerned with prohibition by licensing, not with duties. This type of control is exercised in all countries by administrative action. Every issue of the Board oj Trade Joumal contains changes in the list of products for which the government of the United Kingdom will grant licences. The fact that complete prohibition rather than merely duties is involved requires greater discretion and flexibility in administration. In many respects, if the government did not desire to use the W ar Measures Act, the logical procedure would have been to take power by legislation, place all imports under permit and then proceed by order in council under the aot to set up schedules of imports requiring permits and those for which permits would not be granted.
Out of consideration for parliament the government decided to include the schedules in the legislation and disclose to parliament just what action it is proposed to take. Wide discretion is required by the minister because certain imports may prove to be required for war or other essential services. Restrictions are by tariff items, and even the customs officials cannot name all the articles which may



War Exchange Conservation Act
be included in a single customs item. In the case of such goods as canned vegetables or wearing apparel a serious shortage might conceivably arise if the importation were prohibited and the minister had no power to grant permits at his discretion. In the case of imports under part II it may be necessary to discriminate even between importers in granting permits. One importer may seek a permit to increase his already large stocks of raw materials, while another may apply for a permit merely to replenish exhausted stocks.
I may say also that powers at least as wide as these are vested in ministers by other acts. For instance, there are the powers exercised by the Minister of Finance in connection with the export of gold and the powers exercised by the Minister of National Revenue with respect to export permits. He has a discretion in the matter of export permits, as well as in the matter of import permits for aluminium. These powers can be exercised and will be exercised with care. Powers are now vested in controllers under the Munitions and Supply Act which are much wider than the powers vested here in the Minister of National Revenue.
For these reasons I do not think we should go further than we have. We have divided these items into two parts, part I and part II, and stated to parliament what the intentions of the government are in reference to part I and what the intentions of the government are in reference to part II. I think it is necessary that there should be discretion vested in the minister to deny or grant permits regarding all the items in both parts, the principles upon which he will exercise this being understood and explained to the house.

In order that the record may be clear to anyone reading Hansard, will the minister explain the difference between the treatment which will be meted out in connection with items in part I of schedule one, and in connection with items in part II?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I do not have any idea that we can get away for a great while from the importation of crude petroleum. We are importing $39,000,000 worth of crude petroleum and I would not like to say that the imports of that commodity will ultimately be shut off.

In connection with coal coming from Great Britain or other parts of the empire, just what in the opinion of the minister is going to be the effect of this provision upon the coal mining industry of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have before me a statement from the technical adviser to the coal administrator, the material parts of which are to this effect: Any bituminous coal which we might be able to import from Great Britain would be used entirely in the Quebec and Newfoundland areas where, on account of

War Exchange Conservation Act
increased requirements of the railways and the pulp and paper industry, our own supplies must be supplemented by imports of bituminous coal from the United States. It is not anticipated that importations of British bituminous coal would in any way interfere with the present movement of Nova Scotia coal under subventions, nor would it be necessary under present conditions to extend the market for Nova Scotia coal beyond existing boundaries. A careful study is now being made of the situation with a view to determining the amount of British bituminous coal which might be absorbed in the eastern markets without disturbing present distribution.

I notice that these
observations were directed particularly to Nova Scotia, and I am wondering how the coal mining industry in other parts of Canada will fare. Alberta has quite a coal-mining industry; so has British Columbia, and there are other areas where a less amount of coal mining is done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They would not be affected.

I am glad to know that, but I am under the impression that those in responsible positions in the coal-mining industry are not of the same opinion.
I believe there is need of some sort of conference being called by the government- it should be called here I think-where representatives of the coal-mining industry throughout the country could meet together. In addition to the calling together of representatives of the coal-mining industry of Nova Scotia, Alberta, British Columbia and other coal-mining areas, I believe that labour and other phases of the coal-mining industry should be represented, to determine upon an adequate and proper national coal policy for Canada. I do not believe we have what could be termed a really satisfactory national coal policy.
I have some very big files on coal and all sorts of reports-reports by all sorts of commissions, and reports by various delegations that have come to Ottawa. One report will be along one line and another report along another line. There is a report from a commission created to inquire into anthracite coal, and another report from another commission on some other phase of the coalmining industry. Therefore I believe that a conference should be called at which every part of the coal-mining industry of Canada will be represented, together with the coal committee of the cabinet, and there this whole question could be threshed out with a view to getting down to the business of establishing a really national coal policy. I do not 14873-491
know whether the idea is new to the minister, but I do wish he could say that he favours such a conference. I do not suggest that it be as large as the forthcoming conference on the Sirois report. Nevertheless the coalmining industry of Canada is one of our biggest industries, and I think it is time that something of this sort was done.

In view of the minister's statement that a certain percentage of the coal imported from Great Britain would be utilized in the Quebec market, I wish to say that in my opinion it would seriously affect the Nova Scotia coal-mining industry. Last night the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black) went into the story at length and quoted many figures, but he did not carry the story through. Reading Hansard, one would be led to believe that the coal-mining industry of Nova Scotia had expanded since the introduction of subventions. The reverse is true. By virtue of the subventions given to the coal-mining industry of Nova Scotia, the industry expanded to this extent, that 2,000,000 tons were marketed in Ontario. While the subventions have assisted the industry and enabled Nova Scotia coal to be marketed ' in Ontario, nevertheless during that time there has been a decline in the industry. In that connection I should like to refer to the "Coal Statistics for Canada" for the calendar year 1938, in support of my statement. It states:
Production from Nova Scotia coal mines in 1938 declined to 6,236,417 tons from the 1937 total of 7,256,954 tons. Mines in Oape Breton produced 4,676,730 tons or 14'8 per cent below the 1937 output. Cumberland district produced 713,768 tons compared with 807,651 tons >a year ago. The Inverness output was 7-2 per cent lower at 173,535 tons. In the Pictou district production declined 12-9 per cent to 672,384 tons.
That was in 1938 as compared with 1937, and that decline took place regardless of the fact that we were marketing our coal further west.
There is another matter to which I should like to make reference. I quote further:
Active mines in Nova Scotia in 1938 produced approximately 63 per cent of their possible output; 33*5 per cent of the output loss was due to lack of orders. Causes other than strikes were responsible for a production loss of 3,739,938 tons__
The reason why I put these figures on the record is to show that at the present time the coal-mining industry of Nova Scotia is on the wane. Unemployment has increased, and the figures quoted will show that the reason for that unemployment is lack of markets. We who have been engaged in that industry and do business with the coal

War Exchange Conservation Act
companies know that they have no intention of expanding operations, because of lack of markets; and while I am absolutely in accord with the principle of assisting Britain, I am reasonably sure that the removal of the thirty-five cents duty on British bituminous coal will further affect our production.
At the present time a large part of the war materials being shipped overseas are leaving the ports of Montreal, Halifax and Sydney. I have seen at least 100 boats in convoy leaving a port. Most of those boats arrive without a cargo. By the removal of that thirty-five cents tariff these boats will be enabled to bring back a cargo. Most of them come back with water as ballast, if British bituminous coal is admitted duty free, most of those boats will, in my opinion, bring back cargoes of coal, and we in Nova Scotia cannot compete with it. That has been our experience. Time and again the operators have told us that because of lack of markets they have no intention of expanding the Nova Scotia industry. The statistics of 1938 show that they are away below their possible production, and the consequence is unemployment.
The measure before us is to conserve foreign exchange, and I am absolutely in accord with that object; but I believe that if it is to be effective with respect to the item under discussion, it will have to be carefully administered. I listened to the remarks of the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) having reference to a conference of operators. That has been tried time and time again. Representatives of the east and of the west met in Ottawa and laid down a programme for the purpose of inaugurating a national fuel policy. All we ever got out of it was talk, talk, talk, a whole lot of recommendations, and a good deal of paper; absolutely nothing else.
In my opinion, if we are serious in our endeavour to give Britain a market in this country for her bituminous coal, there is only one way of doing it. Approximately ten million tons of bituminous coal is imported from the United States. The only way of marketing British bituminous coal is to place an embargo on United States bituminous coal which is coming into this country.
Or give them a quota.

Or a quota. Decide upon the amount you intend to take from Britain, bring it in, and put an embargo on the equivalent amount of bituminous coal from the United States. That will have to be done, in my opinion, so as not to interfere with or dislocate markets controlled and handled at the present time by Canadian

operators. There is, in my judgment, no other answer to the problem if we intend to conserve foreign exchange.
I believe that the Nova Scotia industry has already felt the effects of British coal in the Quebec market. During last session there was brought to my attention the fact, which I could not then verify, but which I have since confirmed, that 200,000 tons of British coal which was consigned to France at the time France capitulated was diverted to Canada. I am informed that one of the big mining operators in this country handled and marketed that coal, and the figures which I have seen in one of the local papers reflect, I believe, the effects of the marketing of that coal. According to what I saw in a local newspaper, the Dominion Coal company, the biggest unit of Dominion Iron, Steel and Coal, had an output last month of 22,957 tons less than the output of October, 1939, and 39,396 tons less than the output of October, 1940. That should not be, because there has been created an abnormal market, as a result of the war. The boats constituting the large convoys in and out of a harbour with which I am acquainted are bunkered, and this coal company has done quite a business with the bunker coal. At the same time their output, on account of the additional imports of bunker coal, is in my opinion forty or fifty thousand tons less than it would otherwise be. It is my belief, although I cannot verify it, that that coal was marketed in Quebec, causing the output for the collieries for the last month as compared with the previous month to be down to that extent.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Does the hon. member ascribe the diminished output to any cause other than lack of markets?

I tried to make that clear. I said that 200,000 tons -of British coal which was consigned to France at the time France capitulated came into eastern Canada and was marketed by one of our coal companies. I believe that that tonnage so brought in and placed in the eastern market would be a contributing factor to the monthly decline of the Dominion Coal company.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Has my hon. friend any figures as to the number of tons of coal which were lost on account of the stoppage of work in the collieries?
Yes, I have them right here.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: What are they?

I will read the paragraph in the 1938 report entitled "Coal Statistics for Canada":

War Exchange Conservation Act
Active mines in Nova Scotia in 1938 produced approximately 63 per cent of their possible output; 33-5 per cent of the output loss was due to lack of orders. Causes other than strikes were responsible for a production loss of 3,739,938 tons during the year while strikes accounted for an additional computed loss of 11,651 tons.
I had not any intention of making reference to that particular question, because of what I have heard in the past year from many government officials who have come to our conventions. The Minister of Labour went into 'Nova Scotia, tackled miners' organizations and everyone connected with them and gave them a severe talking to on the question of sporadic strikes and the amount of coal lost as a result of stoppages of work, and so forth. I think the amount of coal lost on account of stoppages of work is insignificant when compared with the amount lost-over three million tons-from other causes. If we are interested in the industry from the viewpoint of production, the other causes should be given as much analysis and investigation as this question of the sporadic strike.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I think my hon. friend knows that the figure of 11,000 tons is entirely incorrect. He must know that.
I do not compile those figures and I have not any way of finding that out.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The hon. member knows that from his own experience.
I am taking the government's word for it. I know there has been doubt cast on it, but I assume these figures are correct. They should be.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: They are not correct.

I want to ask the hon.
member a question, because I know he knows what he is talking about. How many tons is an ordinary day's production of coal? I want to try to estimate how much 11,000 tons would mean in shortages in terms of time. Would it mean more than an hour, or would it mean a day's production? The hon. member said that their loss through strikes was
11,000	tons' production, and I was just trying to ascertain what that means in time. Eleven thousand tons seems to be a very small amount. How much time would that represent? The hon. member is an expert and he must know.

If we take the industry as
a whole, it would amount to practically nothing. One mine produces 4,000 tons a day. With regard to the accuracy of the figures here, that is something I cannot argue; I am accepting them as authentic, because I get them in cold statistics.
My intention in rising was to point out the seriousness of the mining situation in Nova Scotia. It is the basic industry in that province and employs over 100,000 men, and the whole economy of the province is wrapped np in the industry, whose operations are on the wane at the present time. I find, in most of the older mines, that there is no incentive for the companies to go ahead with new programmes. The question of the importation of bituminous coal into the Quebec market, where the minister says more will be used, is a serious one, because that is the only economic market the company has. If it is interfered with or dislocated, it will mean that the company will not go ahead with the programme of making new openings, and an already bad unemployment situation in those areas will be aggravated. We are facing a crisis and it is our intention to help Britain. I am in favour of that. But if we are to bring in any quantity of bituminous coal from Britain there will be no room for the coal from our operators in Canada. We shall have to put a quota on the border and keep out the bituminous coal coming from the United States. Millions of dollars going to that country could be saved.
The government should accept some responsibility with regard to the development of the coal areas in Canada. At the present time Britain is going through a terrific ordeal in consequence of the technique developed by the Germans of attacking town after town in an attempt to make a shambles of the country and to put it out of production. The mining industry there is not immune from destruction and while we are talking about importing bituminous coal from Britain the reverse may be true in six months' time. Canada may have to step in and supply Britain with coal. There are many undeveloped coal fields in Canada, particularly in the part of the country for which I am speaking, and the possibilities of expanding that industry should be probed.
Most of our coal has been shipped by water. It is only a seasonal matter during the winter months. From November until about May the coal is banked and that is a costly operation. An effort should be made to ship Cape Breton coal by rail. There are three factors that make it impossible, and a costly operation, to ship coal by rail, and these should

War Exchange Conservation Act
be removed. In the first place, the assembly yard in Sydney is altogether too small; it should be enlarged; and ninety miles up the line, at Point Tupper, the assembly yard is also very small, being unable to handle much coal. Then there is the strait of Canso to contend with. A train of coal goes through and is shunted around in all directions to make room for it. Taking the train across on the Scotia is a slow operation and is not workable at the present time. It adds much to the cost of transportation by rail.
If the government are sincere in their effort to do something with regard to the industry in that end of the country, a good approach to the problem would be to consider the possibility of either tunneling the strait of Canso-it is only a mile or so-or bridging it, and at the same time enlarging the two yards to which I have referred, thus making it possible for coal to be shipped from that end of the country both summer and winter, and eliminating the necessity of banking the coal. The coal is banked twice, in Sydney and in Montreal, and coal company officials will tell you that this is one of the biggest factors in the question of cost-banking the coal and keeping it from catching fire. That is something which should be considered. The cost would be offset in years to come by the subventions that are now paid. The sum of $2,500,000 a year is now paid by way of assistance, and the industry will need still more assistance in time, or it will shrink to the point where it will take care of only our own domestic market. That seems to be the trend of events at present.
I leave these thoughts with the minister. They are factors that will have to be considered. That part of the country is not getting a fair deal. The people there are living in a completely different world from this part of the dominion. Something must be done for the development of the Nova Scotia coal industry or, I repeat, the industry will shrink to the point where it will take care of only its economic market. I hope the minister will consider these points.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) told the house that there were 100,000 people employed in the coal mining industry in Cape Breton. I am afraid the figure is too large,
The hon. member is wrong in that statement. I said that 100,000 people depended on it.
He said it was the basic industry in Nova Scotia.

So it is.
;Mr. Gillis.]
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon, I did no such thing. I never made that statement. And by the way he might let H. J. Kelley do his own arguing.

I refer to Hansard of
August 6, 1940, page 2549:
Mr. Gillis:	....I know positively without
having to guess about it at all, that no employment has been created for miners since the establishment of subsidies. As a matter of fact the reverse is true. On two occasions I have attempted to paint a picture of conditions in that industry during the past ten years. Coal mining in Nova Scotia is definitely on the way out. Since this session of parliament opened I have had telegrams, wires and letters stating that unemployment was widespread throughout the industry.
I have only a word more to say about subventions. I have been employed by the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation, which controls coal mining in Nova Scotia, for a period of thirty years, and I am very sceptical in regard to the question of subventions. I would advise the government to examine closely into the question whether or not that subvention has been used for the purposes for which it was intended. I have not seen any benefits accruing to the man who produces or digs the coal. That is all I have to say on that point.

War Exchange Conservation Act
That is all right; does that say subventions are no good?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member does not say they are good.
Might I be permitted to correct that statement?
Well, it is in Hansard, I do not know what the hon. member wants to correct.

First, the hon. member made the flat-footed statement that I said subventions were no good. He will find in Hansard that on two other occasions I thanked the government for the assistance given to the Nova Scotia coal-mining industry by way of subventions.
The hon. member has changed his mind.

No; I did not change my mind, I appreciated and do appreciate that assistance, but the point I make is that since the subventions were inaugurated and coal moved westward, that industry has lost other markets somewhere, because according to the government figures production has decreased, and I know that unemployment has increased. I say that I see no benefit accruing to the men who dig the coal, because from 1921 until the present they have lost 37i per cent of their wages, and I cannot see where their standard of living has increased. I say that assistance is necessary, and probably will have to be increased because apparently we are losing the markets somewhere else while we are pushing our coal further west.
Mr. KINLEY; So far as subventions are concerned it is my understanding that the purpose is to enable -the commodity to reach markets which otherwise it could not reach. And the subventions have done just that, because in 1939-40 there were 2,600,000 tons coming to the upper Canadian market and in 1938-39 the amount was 1,300,000 tons.
We must not forget that the government has been pretty generous to the coal-mining industry of Nova Scotia. I have no coal mining in my constituency. The hon. member for Cumberland and the hon. member for Cape Breton South have a local interest in this coal-mining business. I have, however, a general interest -as one who is intensely interested in Nova Scotia generally. In my county we are, however, also interested in foreign markets and we use coal. Canada is a cold country, and to keep warm is an important matter. The government of Canada has been very generous, and the men who represented Nova Scotia here andl who secured
these subventions, with the assistance of the premier of Nova Scotia, ought to be commended. The subventions are splendid. I am told by men who know, that the industry could not survive as a national industry without the subvention, so I hope it will be continued.
With regard to British coal I am told that the price at the present time is advancing in Great Britain and freight rates are also high so that you really must have some special concession in order to get coal at all from Great Britain. I am informed that during this week immense quantities of coal have come up into the province of Quebec from the United States for the purpose of supplying war-time industries. Look at what this United States coal has to face. There is the exchange which is around 20 per cent; there is a 10 per cent excise tax, and the duty. It seems to me that might be called adequate protection. When this coal comes in in such quantities over such hurdles it is hard to talk on economic grounds.
I am told that there is not the slightest danger to Cape Breton coal or Nova Scotia coal. The cheapest coal to mine is in Cape Breton; the mainland mines bring up the average cost of production. But I am told that there is not the slightest danger because there is room for all. During this winter time any English or Welsh coal that will come to the maritime ports cannot get up the St. Lawrence on account of ice, and it will not get the $2 subvention to Montreal or $2.50 to Toronto. Surely that is a preferred position for the industry in this country. I think the hon. member should say that this government has done well by the coal-mining industry of Nova Scotia.
Let us look a little further. Under the legislation now before the committee we are restricting petroleum products. Some time ago there was an order in council which prohibited the use of petroleum for heating purposes in this country under certain conditions. That is all to the benefit of the coalmining industry. We are putting back the clock, as it were, in the interest of the coalmining industry; that industry is being helped because it is in the national interest. It occurs to me that my hon. friend is using a local economic problem in arguing against an item that is inserted because of the national interest and with an international aspect.
This legislation is for a purpose, that of stabilizing exchange as between the three great countries concerned in this war. It seems to me that if there is anything we can do in order to stop what might be called a financial traffic jam in the flow of money between the three countries, it should be done. All

War Exchange Conservation Act
three will be benefited; and surely we in Nova Scotia need not put the red light of danger before this parliament in connection with that matter. It may be we should put the orange light of caution on so that we may watch it in future. But I think that with the reduction of 35 cents duty a ton on coal, there will not be very many people hurt.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South said that the 3 per cent excise duty was taken off United States coal when we raised the subvention a year or two ago. That is only 5 cents a ton; it is very little. The whole problem resolves itself into one of whether we must have teamwork for the interests of the whole country. If the British can send us some coal, if only for ballast for ships that go over there with the goods we produce, it is better than having them return to Canada empty. It will also mean that perhaps we shall have British coal, which will help the exchange situation, instead of more coal from our southern neighbours who are rich in exchange.

I tried to have my remarks relevant to the matter before the committee. In 1939, approximately $18,000,000 worth of bituminous coal came in from the United States. I have tried to be patriotic. If we are going to market British coal in Canada on the basis of conserving foreign exchange, then we should exclude as much as possible of the United States product, and give the preference to Great Britain. The coal should be zoned, so that it would not dislocate the present Canadian market.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It will not.

I am not a coal expert; I cannot quote figures, or anything of that kind, but I am from a province which to-day produces the second largest amount of coal in Canada. I refer to Alberta. It is safe to say that if we had the markets we ought to have in Canada, and that if we have any sort of national policy, then certainly we have the capacity in Alberta to produce very much more coal than any other province, or, in fact, than all the other provinces put together.
The measure with which we are dealing has for its purpose the conservation of foreign exchange, and has particular reference to the exchange position with the United States. I have before me some figures submitted by the western fuel dealers association, and I believe I may assume they are correct because they check with the figures appearing in the "Canada Year Book." In 1939, we imported from the United States 2,605.735 tons of anthracite. It may be argued that anthracite

is needed, that it cannot be supplanted, and that we cannot put bituminous coal in its place. The value of that coal is placed at about $27,000,000. In addition to that, we imported 9,836,110 tons of bituminous coal to a value of almost $63,000,000. If we add the $27,000,000 to the $63,000,000 we have a total of $90,000,000. Then, to that total could be added United States coke to the value of about $3,000,000.
If the government are really serious about this business of trying to save foreign exchange, surely I have shown a field which should be carefully explored by them. I may be asked what can be done. True, our coal is under subvention at the present time. I would, however, suggest to the government that, on account of the wheat situation in the west, a much smaller amount of wheat is moving along our railways. For that reason I assume rolling stock would be available for the movement of coal. I submit that the government might very well take up with the railways the matter of moving more coal to the east, and of having the railways reduce the present rate of $8, one which I believe applies to most of Alberta. If it were reduced only to the extent of 50 cents a ton, such a reduction would enable Alberta coal to go farther into Ontario.
My personal view is that it would be good business if the present subvention of $2.50 a ton were raised to $3, to serve that portion of Ontario which is not now covered by the $2.50 rate. I suggest that the government might very well take this matter into consideration, and for this reason: From all sides of the House of Commons we have heard discussion respecting national unity. It is admitted that practically all the war contracts are placed in the two central provinces. We in the west and the maritimes in the east are not receiving many contracts. We are not complaining, particularly, because, handicapped through lack of power, we have not as good facilities to offer. The fact remains, however, that we have some facilities which might be used. But if power is necessary, and since it is recognized that coal is a big factor in the development of power, I believe the part of Canada from which I come might be given further consideration in connection with the development of war industries.
My point is this: At the two extreme ends of Canada we have not the necessary industries. We still have a great deal of unemployment, much of which is in the coal-mining areas. In the winter time many of our farmers act as both farmers and coal miners. Many of the farmers are capable of doing

War Exchange Conservation Act
coal-mining operations, and in that way they fill in their time and help fill out their limited incomes.
When we are thinking of national unity, I suggest that this is something we might keep in mind. The government should try to devise a policy which will give the people in the section of western Canada from which I come an opportunity to do something worth while. The more tons of United States coal which, through a measure of this kind, can be kept out, just to that extent do we save United States exchange. That is the purpose behind the measure before the committee. I leave the matter with the government, so that they may think about it.

I was absent from the house this afternoon when the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. McCann) challenged the statement I had made earlier. Therefore I ask to be allowed to revert to the discussion of item ex 152 in the schedule.
The hon. member states that I deliberately failed to give the committee the proper information. Then he refers to his having interjected something into the debate of a few' days ago. The hon. member states that when the leader of the. opposition was speaking, he interjected that it took twenty times the quantity of ordinary tomato juice as sold in cans to produce the same amount of vitamin C as is produced by orange juice sold in cans. The hon. member is reported at page 654 of Hansard as follows:
But not in the same quantity. It takes twenty times as much tomato juice to give the same quantity of vitamins.
The hon. member makes no reference to its being in cans. In my statement today I clearly stated, in two paragraphs, that I was referring to juice from sieved Canadian canned tomatoes. I picked them out, specially, because I did not think it was too much to ask Canadian housewives at this time, when economy is necessary, and when the Minister of Finance is asking us to tighten our belts, to spend a little time in putting tomato juice through a sieve, particularly when the vitamin content is considerably increased by so doing.
If the hon. member prefers, I will give the figures respecting canned tomato juice which has not been put through a sieve. The amount of milligrammes per ounce in that instance stands at 4.9, using the figure given for the best brand selected from eight or ten different brands of tomato juice. If we take that as against 11.3 of orange juice, it gives the vitamin content of orange juice as being about 2^ times more than tomato juice.
Of the one vitamin?

Vitamin C, which is an important vitamin and one of great importance in nutrition. I have given these figures from table 3 of the report referred to, which has to do with the content of vitamin C in canned tomato juice. My hon. friend referred to it to-night, but he did not refer to it as canned tomato juice in his speech the other day.
I should like to give the average vitamin content which is given here in case I am accused again of not giving all the information. The average vitamin content of all brands of tomato juice is 3-6 milligrammes per ounce, while the average of all orange juice brands from various parts of the United States is 12-5 milligrammes; that is the average vitamin content in orange juice is less than four times greater than in canned tomato juice. I fail to understand why an hon. member who, I am sure, is interested in helping Canadians to dispose of their products and who, I am also sure, is interested in educating the public in the nutritional value of the tomato, should take the stand he has. The tomato is grown in every garden in Canada, by poor as well as by those able to afford orange juice. I would have thought that he would be interested in even exaggerating the importance of our own product.
Who shall decide when doctors disagree?
I am quoting from a report of an investigation which was undertaken in Toronto for this specific purpose. I think the evidence is perfectly clear and I leave it to the committee.

The hon. gentleman has referred to the value of juices in an evident attempt to extol the Canadian tomato. He is to be complimented upon that, but I want him to know that in Nova Scotia we think the apple is superior and we recommend it to the people of this country.
Coming back to this coal question, I want to say that with resolution 6 we went to special lengths to assist Canadian industries which are a little hard pressed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend seems to have the wrong idea. It is not a case of relieving industries, it is a case of getting industries to do a job for us and making a tax concession if they will do that job.

I am glad the minister brought that to my attention. In order to get these industries to do the



War Exchange Conservation Act
job efficiently, we have to guarantee them a profit. We are guaranteeing them a profit of 24-4 per cent-I think that was the minister's statement-above their normal profit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not want to get into any altercation over the Excess Profits Tax Act at this time. There is no guarantee of a profit to industry. If there was any guarantee, there would be no difficulty. Many of these companies risk as much as half a million or a million dollars. They cannot, unless some concession is made, make these large capital investments to meet a demand in what may prove to be a temporary market. I do not know whether they can or not, but they will not. I do not wish hon. members or the country to think we are taking power to hand out concessions to industries because we want to put them in the profit-making class or guarantee them a profit. Not at all, it is a question of asking them if they will produce so much exchange for us, in which event we will make certain concessions in connection with their depreciation or depletion or by way of tax credit.

Nevertheless it is a concession to those industries. As the minister says, they may not make a profit, but if they do make a profit they are entitled to 20-4 per cent above the normal profit which they have made in the past three years. We take 75 per cent of the excess profits, but we leave them with 25 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Twenty-five per cent of
what?

Twentyfive per cent above the average for the past three years, which was used as a basis. The minister corrected the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and said that it worked out to about 20-4 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: From what the hon. gentleman says, I am not at all sure that he knows what the 25 per cent is of. It is 20-5 per cent of the profit. That is, if they make a dollar profit, this tax takes 79i cents.
Of the excess profit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If they make that profit
over and above what they made before.
I understand that perfectly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Then the provinces usually
take some more.

But that
leaves them a good margin above their ordinary profit. It depends, of course, upon the business they do.

The point I want to make is that these industries are given every possible assistance in order that their production may be continued. Surely the minister would not say that we have not sufficient coal in Canada to take care of our requirements. As the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Casselman) and the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) pointed out, we have an abundance of coal. What I am worrying about is why we should want to import more coal from Great Britain when we have thousands of people unemployed.
At Drumheller in my constituency there is one of the greatest coal industries in Canada. Every time I go there, these men come to me and wish to know what the government is doing. They say that all they want is a chance to work. I shall have to go back after this session and be faced with their questions as to why this government is letting in this coal from Great Britain. These men are sitting along the railroad tracks without any work to do. I cannot explain to these men that they are supposed to remain on the relief rolls, that their families are supposed to continue to suffer because they cannot get enough work to buy food and clothing. Yet here we are reducing the tariff so that coal from Great Britain may come in. I am not against coal coming in from Great Britain because we should give that country every assistance, but we should be consistent in our actions.
As the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Kinley) has just said, it is quite possible that coal will be brought from Great Britain as ballast. It might prove to be in the interests of the shipowners to bring coal in as ballast, and if that is done the eastern mines will not be able to compete. It will only aggravate the situation in the east, which is already getting beyond our control. If there was not enough coal here, then I would say, bring it in from Great Britain.
We should shut off coal coming from the United States and thereby save in foreign exchange. I spoke at some length last session in connection with conserving foreign exchange by this action. If I remember the figures rightly, we would save something like $50,000,000 in foreign exchange if we produced our coal requirements in Canada instead of bringing them in from the United States. This would seem to be commendable action for the government to take. If that were done, then I would have no objection to coal coming in from Great Britain. But when we allow all this coal to come in from Great Britain and thus aggravate our labour troubles, it does not seem logical to me.

War Exchange Conservation Act
Then we have a situation in the west with regard to wheat. We are now going to shut off the farmers; they are not to be allowed to make a profit of any kind. The coal miners are now going to be shut off and not be allowed to make a profit of any kind. The Minister of Labour (Mr. McLarty) is going to have difficulties on his hands because of the increased importations of coal that will be coming in, and I think he might very well review this legislation with respect to its effect on the coal industry of Canada. I think he should at least restrict the amount of coal coming in from the United States by the tonnage that we shall be importing from Great Britain. These importations will only aggravate the present unfavourable conditions in this whole industry. If we are going to preach unity to the people of Canada, let us be logical about the whole matter. While coal importations from Great Britain may not affect us very much in the west, the coal industry in eastern Canada is going to be seriously affected. Coal is a national problem, and I think the government would be well advised to formulate a national coal policy for the benefit of all Canada and not for just one section of it.
